title: Career Roadmap— B.Sc. Computer Science → IT Support Engineer
summary: An IT Support Engineer helps people and organizations keep their computers, applications, networks, and IT systems working reliably. The role combines technical troubleshooting, customer communication, system administration, and security awareness.

blocks.text: An IT Support Engineer helps people and organizations keep their computers, applications, networks, and IT systems working reliably. The role combines technical troubleshooting, customer communication, system administration, and security awareness.

A B.Sc. Computer Science graduate can enter this career through an IT support trainee, service desk analyst, desktop support technician, or junior IT support engineer position. A four-year degree is not generally required for entry-level support roles, although employer requirements vary.
What you will do

items.text: Diagnose hardware, software, login, and connectivity problems.
Install, configure, and maintain computers and business applications.
Manage user accounts, permissions, and password resets.
Resolve support tickets and document solutions.
Escalate complex network, server, cloud, or security issues to specialist teams.

blocks.text: Typical entry roles
IT Support Trainee, Service Desk Analyst, Desktop Support Technician
Work settings
IT services, corporate IT teams, MSPs, hospitals, education, and technology firms
Core strengths
Troubleshooting, communication, patience, documentation
Career directions
System administration, networking, cloud support, cybersecurity

rows.text: IT Support Trainee / Service Desk Analyst
IT Support Engineer / Desktop Support Engineer
Windows, devices, users, and business applications
Advanced troubleshooting, Active Directory, networks, automation
Infrastructure, access controls, monitoring, and administration
Senior Systems Engineer / Cloud Support / IT Operations Lead

blocks.text: These are indicative career stages, not guaranteed promotion timelines.
The plan below assumes a three-year B.Sc. programme. Adapt it to your university's syllabus and the time remaining before graduation.
Year 1
Foundations
Build computer and operating-system fundamentals

blocks.label: Learn computer hardware
blocks.text: CPU, RAM, storage, peripherals, BIOS/UEFI, and drivers.

items.text: Understand Windows installation, configuration, updates, user profiles, and basic troubleshooting.

blocks.label: Learn Linux basics
blocks.text: terminal commands, files, permissions, and processes.

blocks.label: Study computer networks
blocks.text: IP addresses, DNS, DHCP, routers, switches, and Wi-Fi.

items.text: Practise professional communication and clear technical documentation.

blocks.label: Practical outcome
blocks.text: Set up a Windows and Linux lab using a spare computer or virtual machines and document common issues and solutions.
Year 2
Administration
Learn enterprise IT support

items.text: Practise Windows troubleshooting through Event Viewer, Task Manager, Services, and Device Manager.
Learn Windows Server concepts, Active Directory, user groups, and Group Policy.
Use PowerShell and basic Bash for repetitive administrative tasks.
Practise networking diagnostics using ping, ipconfig, tracert, nslookup, and netstat.
Learn ticket lifecycle, priority assignment, SLAs, escalation, and knowledge-base writing.
Understand endpoint protection, patching, backups, MFA, and least-privilege access.

blocks.label: Practical outcome
blocks.text: Build a simulated company IT environment with user accounts, shared folders, access permissions, and troubleshooting documentation.
Year 3
Job readiness
Convert technical knowledge into employable experience

items.text: Practise real-world help-desk scenarios and timed troubleshooting exercises.
Learn IT service management concepts and a ticketing platform such as Jira Service Management or ServiceNow.
Explore Microsoft 365 administration and cloud fundamentals.
Create PowerShell scripts for routine checks and system inventory.
Complete a practical IT support project and maintain a portfolio.
Prepare a resume, practise support interviews, and apply for internships and entry-level roles.

blocks.label: Practical outcome
blocks.text: Demonstrate that you can diagnose, resolve, document, and escalate common user and system issues.
Prioritize these skills in order. You do not need to master every enterprise tool before applying for your first role.

Project 1 — Desktop Troubleshooting Handbook

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Beginner
Create documented solutions for 20 common problems, including slow computers, failed updates, printer issues, application crashes, and login errors.

blocks.label: Deliverable
blocks.text: A searchable troubleshooting guide with symptoms, diagnostic steps, root causes, and verified fixes.
Project 2 — Small Office IT Lab

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Intermediate
Set up virtual machines, create sample users and groups, configure shared folders and permissions, and test access restrictions. Use a Windows Server evaluation environment where available.

blocks.label: Deliverable
blocks.text: Network diagram, setup guide, test cases, and troubleshooting log.
Project 3 — IT Inventory and Health Report

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Intermediate
Use PowerShell to collect permitted system information, such as hostname, operating-system version, disk capacity, and available storage. Export a report to CSV.

blocks.label: Deliverable
blocks.text: Script, sample output, instructions, and a brief explanation of error handling.
Project 4 — Help-Desk Ticket Simulation

blocks.label: Level
blocks.text: Job-ready portfolio
Create 30–50 fictional support tickets. Categorize incidents, set priorities, record troubleshooting steps, document escalation, and write resolution notes.

blocks.label: Deliverable
blocks.text: A sample ticket dashboard, SLA tracking, and a knowledge base.
Use fictional data; do not include real users' credentials or company information.

blocks.label: Recommended capstone
blocks.text: Combine Projects 2, 3, and 4 into a simulated small-company IT support environment. This demonstrates systems knowledge, automation, and service-desk workflow in one portfolio.
Choose certifications based on your target job rather than collecting many certificates.

rows.text: Incident management, service delivery, and ITSM terminology

blocks.text: Official learning resources:

items.text: Microsoft Learn — Windows, Microsoft 365, PowerShell, and Azure.
Cisco Skills for All — networking and cybersecurity fundamentals.
CompTIA A+ certification — certification objectives and exam information.
Ubuntu documentation — Linux installation and administration.
PowerShell documentation — scripting and system administration.

blocks.text: Certification exams may involve fees. Check the current syllabus, eligibility, and cost before paying. You can start learning with free resources and hands-on labs.
Start applying once you can troubleshoot common Windows issues, explain basic networking, and demonstrate at least one practical project. Do not wait until you have completed every certification.

blocks.label: Where to look
blocks.text: IT services companies, managed service providers (MSPs), corporate IT departments, educational institutions, hospitals, and businesses with large internal IT teams.

Potential employers to research include TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Tech Mahindra, Accenture, Cognizant, and IBM. This is a list of examples to investigate, not a claim that they currently have openings.
Weekly application routine
Tailor your resume to the job description and highlight hands-on work, not just course completion.
Practise explaining the diagnostic process, not merely memorizing definitions.

rows.text: A computer is running slowly. What do you do?
Check resource usage, startup apps, disk space, updates, and relevant logs
A user cannot access the internet. How do you troubleshoot?
Check connectivity, IP configuration, DNS, gateway, and scope of the outage
What is the difference between DNS and DHCP?
DNS resolves names; DHCP provides network configuration such as IP addresses
A user cannot log in. What do you check?
Account status, credentials, connectivity, permissions, and relevant authentication errors
How would you handle an angry user?
Listen, clarify impact, communicate clearly, document, and follow up
When should you escalate a ticket?
When the issue exceeds your permissions or expertise, breaches risk thresholds, or requires specialist intervention

blocks.text: Never make unapproved changes to production systems. Follow company procedures, protect user data, and document actions.

sections.heading: Skills to develop for long-term growth

blocks.text: Once you become comfortable with L1 support, choose a specialization rather than remaining limited to repetitive password resets and basic troubleshooting.
Systems administration
Develop Windows Server, Active Directory, Group Policy, Linux, backup, and monitoring skills.
Networking
Progress into subnetting, VLANs, routing, firewalls, VPNs, and network monitoring.
Cloud and infrastructure support
Learn cloud identity, virtual machines, monitoring, access control, and cloud troubleshooting.
Cybersecurity
Build knowledge of endpoint security, identity management, patching, incident response, and security logs.
A postgraduate degree is not normally necessary to begin an IT support career. Consider further education when it supports a clear next step.

blocks.label: M.Sc. Computer Science / IT
blocks.text: Broader computing and systems knowledge.

blocks.label: MCA
blocks.text: A possible path toward software and application-oriented roles, subject to programme eligibility.

blocks.label: M.Sc. Cybersecurity
blocks.text: Relevant if progressing toward security operations or security engineering.

blocks.label: Cloud and networking certifications
blocks.text: Often more directly aligned with infrastructure-support specializations than an additional degree.
Days 1–30
Foundation
Learn Windows troubleshooting, hardware fundamentals, basic Linux, and networking. Start a troubleshooting journal and solve common issues in a safe lab.
Days 31–60
Practice
Build the small-office lab, practise ticket documentation, learn PowerShell basics, and publish your first two projects.
Days 61–90
Apply
Finish the help-desk simulation, prepare your resume, rehearse interview scenarios, and apply consistently to relevant internships and entry-level roles.
Ready to apply?

blocks.label: Recommendation
blocks.text: For a B.Sc. Computer Science graduate, prioritize Windows troubleshooting, networking fundamentals, ticket handling, and practical lab experience first. Then add PowerShell and Microsoft 365 administration. This combination gives you a focused foundation for entry-level IT support and a route into systems, cloud, or cybersecurity roles.
